extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law scholars, judges, and practitioners concerned with APA notice-and-comment and judicial review of agency rulemaking
extracted.subtask_short: judicial review of good cause determinations
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and prescribe the standard and institutional allocation for reviewing agency invocations of the APA good cause exception to notice-and-comment rulemaking; the paper argues courts should review such determinations de novo and explains why legislative or executive fixes are unlikely or undesirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No deference to agency assertions of good cause (de novo review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should afford no deference to an agency’s determination that good cause exists; reviewing courts should apply de novo review to agency invocations of the APA’s good cause exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounded in the APA’s text, structure, and objectives and consistent with §706; the standard balances public participation, agency flexibility, public safety, and judicial administrability. The D.C. Circuit in Sorenson supports rejecting deference to agency interpretations of the APA; agencies lack the same specialized expertise regarding the APA as they do over statutes they administer. Courts should not accept an exception merely because the agency says it applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts are well positioned to police good cause use
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review is the most appropriate institutional mechanism to police agency use of the good cause exception because courts are experts in procedural fair play and can enforce compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies (e.g., Raso) and surveys of rule drafters show agencies are sensitive to litigation risk and judicial doctrines; courts routinely interpret and enforce procedural rules and can therefore shape agency behavior even if they review only a fraction of invocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of the APA’s good cause text is not realistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional amendment of the APA’s good cause exception is highly improbable given historical infrequency of APA amendments and current political polarization and legislative dysfunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past failed amendments and the APA’s quasi-constitutional status reduce political appetite for change; universal applicability across agencies makes consensus harder and amendments politically costly; therefore statutory amendment is an impractical solution to perceived agency abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amending the statute is not desirable (likely ineffective or harmful)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if Congress amended the good cause language, modest textual changes are unlikely to affect legal outcomes and could unduly constrain agencies or be rendered surplusage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars find differences in wording (e.g., 'imminent peril' vs federal phrasing) often do not change judicial outcomes; courts’ evaluations are largely untethered to precise statutory text; overly restrictive statutory language risks eliminating needed flexibility for agencies facing unforeseeable factual permutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer agency-specific statutory triggers over a uniform APA amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where change is desirable, agency-specific statutes (that add or remove procedural requirements) are a more practicable and precise approach than amending the APA’s general good cause exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency-specific statutes can codify procedural triggers tied to fact patterns endemic to that agency, are politically easier to negotiate, and avoid the problem of drafting universally applicable emergency exceptions for more than 100 diverse agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional oversight mechanisms are limited and inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools Congress has besides amendment—reporting requirements, GAO investigations, spending power, Congressional Review Act—have been insufficient to police agency invocations of good cause in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees have limited time and resources and tend to focus on high-salience rules; exemptions of good-cause rules from statutory reporting (e.g., RFA, UMRA) reduce congressional notice; enforcement relies on political incentives that often do not prioritize procedural compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive oversight is unlikely to curb improper good cause use
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive branch (including OIRA) is poorly suited to policing procedural compliance because it focuses on substantive priorities and many agencies (notably independent agencies) are exempt from its most potent tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA reviews relatively few emergency rulemakings and typically assesses substance rather than procedural compliance; presidential attention tends to prioritize policy substance over APA procedural fidelity, and resource constraints limit comprehensive oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation risk and judicial enforcement incentivize agency compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are sensitive to the 'shadow' of judicial review; increased litigation risk correlates with higher procedural compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raso's empirical work finds agencies comply more with procedures as litigation risk rises and that agencies with lower litigation exposure avoid notice-and-comment more often; surveys of rule drafters indicate 87% consider subsequent judicial review when drafting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposals to tighten good cause (imminent peril, precise criteria, brief statement standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars have proposed replacing or refining the federal good cause standard (e.g., adopting the 'imminent peril' state standard, specifying circumstances justifying good cause, or requiring a 'brief statement of reasons' explaining how prepromulgation procedures would frustrate substantial harm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Boliek advocating 'imminent peril,' Kim proposing express criteria (immediate necessity for public health/safety/welfare, notice would impair effectiveness, delay would frustrate legislative policies), and Yates suggesting a brief-statement standard detailing how identifiable measurable prepromulgation procedures would frustrate substantial harm. The article critiques these as either unlikely to change judicial outcomes or infeasible to craft comprehensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exempting good-cause rules from reporting reduces oversight; states sometimes increase emergency reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies invoke good cause they are often excused from significant statutory reporting requirements (e.g., RFA, UMRA), which diminishes congressional awareness and scrutiny of such rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lack of notice makes legislative policing harder; by contrast some states adopt increased reporting requirements for emergency rules (e.g., COLO. REV. STAT. § 24-4-103(3); MINN. STAT. § 14.388; OHIO REV. CODE ANN. § 119.03(C)), reflecting a model where political oversight compensates for lack of public participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies lack interpretive authority over the APA; deference doctrines are inappropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies do not possess special interpretive authority regarding the APA itself, so courts should not defer to agency interpretations when assessing procedural questions under the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D.C. Circuit decisions (e.g., Sorenson, Envirocare) and scholarship note that when a statute like the APA is administered across many agencies, courts should not defer to any single agency’s interpretation; this supports de novo review of good cause invocations under §706.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply APA §706 as governing standards to hold unlawful agency action lacking good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court instructs that the 'standards to be applied on review' of agency actions are governed by §706 of the APA; under §706(2)(D) courts should 'hold unlawful and set aside agency action, findings, and conclusions' that fail to satisfy procedural requirements like good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most natural reading of §706 directs courts to give no deference to legal conclusions that good cause exists; courts should use §706's remedial authority to enforce procedural compliance rather than deferring to agencies.
